en: 1. The Chapter on Knowledge (Jñānādhikāra).
Having somehow attained the service of Maheśvara and desiring to benefit even ordinary people,
I shall establish that recognition (pratyabhijñā) which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections.

I, who have obtained the exceedingly rare fortune of His service solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord, feeling ashamed of my solitary prosperity, cause even this entire world to recognize its own Master by means of the method to be described hereafter, so that I may be satisfied by the attainment of the ultimate goal.
In the Great Lord, who is the agent, the knower, one's own self, and eternally established—who, being non-inert, could effect either a negation or an affirmation [of Him]? 1.1.2.

For all [beings], there exists knowledge and action belonging to that which is self-established, ancient, and whose singular form is the subject (*pramātṛ*); which is self-luminous; whose establishment is embraced by the fact that the accomplishment of all respective objects would otherwise be impossible; and which is the support for the accomplishment of all objects for its own self.
Sovereignty is established through one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Therefore, the effort regarding the proof or refutation of God belongs only to the insentient.
However, because this [Self] is not perceived despite being seen due to the power of delusion,
this recognition is demonstrated by means of manifesting its inherent capacity.

However, although this Lord is established through self-awareness alone, because He is not easily grasped due to the delusion caused by *māyā*, merely a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form of a firm conviction is demonstrated here by proclaiming His extraordinary power and knowledge.
For thus, the support of insentient beings is dependent upon the living;
knowledge and action are considered the life-force of those beings that possess life.
IPV: There is a twofold division of entities based on the distinction between the insentient and the sentient.
Among these, the establishment of the nature of the insentient resides in the living being;
furthermore, for those who are living, their state of being alive—that is, life itself—consists precisely of cognition and action.
In that regard, knowledge is self-established, whereas action, being dependent upon the body, may be perceived even by others; through that [action], the other's knowledge is inferred.
In the case of living beings, action—which culminates in the movement of the body—is perceived here [in oneself] through direct perception;

whereas cognition, though self-evident, is established in another person only through [observing] their action. Thus, it is established that the Self, which is cognized as "I" by both oneself and others, is indeed known through self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
It is only because its nature is obscured by the power of *māyā* that such a misconception arises.
Thus ends the introduction.
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on knowledge.

Now, is it not the case that one cognition has the appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while the other is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and is associated with verbal expression; yet these two are not manifold? (IPK 1.2.1)
Since no eternal observer whatsoever appears here [in this cognition],
even this perception of "I" terminates in the body and so forth.

The opponents say: "Knowledge is one; they describe it as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), having the nature of an experience of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) with a clear manifestation.
But another [kind of knowledge], which has many divisions such as memory, doubt, and imagination through the coloring of words, is designated as conceptual (*vikalpa*).
Neither of these two is tenable, because nothing other than knowledge whose nature is consciousness (*bodha*) is perceived as being related to it."
What is this stable-natured self?
Even by means of the verbalizable notion of "I," no experiencer whatsoever is perceived by people as something transcending the objects of cognition such as the body and so forth.
Furthermore, if experience were to perish, how could there be a memory that conforms to it? Moreover, if the self were the experiencer, it would not be eternal. (IPK 1.2.3)

Objection: Since the previous experience has perished at the time of recollection, how could a memory arise possessing the quality of being supported by the previous experience of an object, if the awareness of that experience does not persist even then?
And that awareness which persists through multiple moments is precisely the self-experiencer.

Even if a self exists, since perception has perished, by what means could there be memory of objects previously perceived through that [perception]? Or rather, memory occurs only with respect to those very objects where there was experience. (IPK 1.2.4)

[Objection: Since the appearance of an object has perished, there is no object here for memory to rely upon; thus, even though the self exists as a single cognitive essence, memory would be entirely without an object, which would result in the cessation of worldly discourse.
[Response: If it is argued that memory possesses an object by virtue of the experience of an object, even if that object is non-existent;
For since memory arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience, what purpose would there be for a persisting self (*ātman*), which is like a useless internal tumor? (IPK 1.2.5)

From experience, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises, and from that impression, memory is born; reproducing that prior experience, it manifests that experience with its previously apprehended object.
Thus, what is the use of a persisting self (*ātman*), since even in the theory of a self, the existence of mental impressions is admitted, and by those alone, the result is established?

Therefore, when phenomena have ceased, since their specific nature remains unchanged, memory would be established through a mere mental impression; thus, the rememberer would be a mere conceptual construct, just like the original perceiver.

Moreover, the self is of no use even as the substratum for distinct properties such as pleasure, pain, and cognition; for that which is undivided by distinct properties and has not undergone any modification cannot be active with respect to memory, just as it is not active when it is merely a witness.
Therefore, the notion that "the self remembers" is a mere conceptual construction.
If cognition is of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), then why is it not eternal like the Self?
On the other hand, if it is insentient (*jaḍa*), how can it have the capacity to illuminate objects?

If cognition has consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), then—just like the self—it would follow that it is eternal and so forth, due to its connection with the entry of objects, qualities, space, and time.
If, on the other hand, it were insentient (*jaḍatva*), how could it be the illumination of an object?

Just as the intellect assumes the form of the object, so too does it assume the consciousness of the self; for that very intellect is non-inert, since if it were inert, there would be no manifestation of the object.
Objection: Knowledge is the intellect (*buddhi*).

Although it is insentient (*jaḍa*), just as it bears the reflection of the form of the object, so too does it bear the reflection of the consciousness of the Self; therefore, this manifestation of the object would likewise result in the intellect having the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatā*).
Thus, although knowledge exists, it does not belong to another,
because that is logically untenable;
action, however, exists neither in its own nature nor as something belonging to another.
Action also consists in the arising of an object, such as the body, in various locations and so forth;
it is not [action] because of seeing something else. Furthermore, that [action] is neither unitary nor is it appropriate for a single [entity] to be successive.

Objection: Even action (*kriyā*), consisting of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) and having parts arranged in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, is not tenable, because that which is successive and touches multiple points of time cannot possess a single identity.
Nor is it tenable for its substratum to be both pervasive across a temporal sequence and of a single nature;
rather, that action consists solely of forms such as the transformation of going (*gamana-pariṇāma*).
However, in the case of the body and so forth, this is merely their prior existence in various distinct places and times, since nothing else beyond this is perceived.
In each respective case, it is observed that "when this is present, that comes to be";
there is no other relation than that of cause and effect.
IPV: There is experience only to this extent—that when the prior exists, the subsequent exists.
And there is no relationship between action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka) distinct from that, because nothing separate from it is perceived.
Apart from the relation of cause and effect, there is no other such characteristic of entities.
Because that which resides in two [places] has multiple forms, because what is established is independent of anything else,
and because dependence on another is impossible, the agent too is merely a conceptual construction.

[The opponent replies: A relation resides in two things, and it is not logical for it to exist in both by means of a single essence. Furthermore, a relation cannot consist of mutual dependence between two things already established in themselves, nor can it be a form of dependence between two things that are each restricted to their own nature. Therefore, just as the state of being a knower is imagined [in the Self], so too is the state of being an agent; how then can the Self be the Lord of all?
True; however, memory-cognition, though it arises based on the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience and resides within the self, does not perceive the present experience. (IPK 1.3.1)

Objection: Even though memory arises from the awakening of impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience, it is merely self-cognizing because it is grounded solely in the self; however, due to the absence of any penetration (*āveśa*) by the prior experience, it cannot logically establish the object previously experienced.

Vision is self-manifesting and cannot be known by anything else, just as the vision of form [is not known by another vision]. As for the fact that [the cognition of] taste arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), its similarity [to the case of form] does not establish that [taste] is perceived [by the same means]. (IPK 1.3.2)

For every cognition (*jñapti*) is of a single nature consisting solely of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and not of another awareness; [if it were otherwise], there would be two kinds [of awareness].

If the cognition of color and the cognition of taste were mutually aware of one another, there would also be a mutual awareness of their respective objects, and consequently, there would be no restriction of the sense faculties.

Since [the subsequent cognition] arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, it possesses mere similarity to that [prior experience], but it is not an apprehension of the prior experience itself.
Even its similarity cannot be determined.

Now, even if memory does not have that [past object] as its objective domain, it is claimed that it has a perceived object due to error because it terminates in that; this is inconsistent. (IPK 1.3.3)

Nor, moreover, is memory that which has as its object [the past] because it determines, through error, a prior experience and its object—such as silver in the case of mother-of-pearl—as if they were not being experienced [at the present time].

How can there even be memory? And how can there be the persistence of an object for that which is erroneous? Furthermore, why is dependence upon the latencies of prior experience asserted? (IPK 1.3.4)
IPV: Since the previous experience is not manifest, it is not logical for memory to consist merely of a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) when its object has been forgotten.

Nor can there be a re-establishment of a previously experienced object through error; for if the error does not touch upon the previous experience, what grounds are there for asserting that such an error—possessing a character distinct from that experience—is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)?
If the determination were an error, the object could not be established by means of that which is insentient;
therefore, since it is not insentient, it must rest upon its own internal representation, and thus the object cannot be established from that [representation].
IPV: It is *adhyavasāya* (determinate cognition) alone that establishes the object through error, and not self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).

Moreover, how could that [self-awareness], being insentient (*jaḍa*), be the cause for the establishment of an object? Even if it were of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it would either manifest only a past object or only the internal reflection of its own non-external self; in either case, it would not be the cause of that [establishment].
Thus, if cognitions were mutually distinct and lacked mutual awareness, the continuity of worldly existence— which arises from the synthesis of those cognitions— would perish.
IPV: Cognitions are established solely within their own self and, being of the nature of self-awareness, are not perceivable by another.
How can there be worldly transaction—which culminates in the instruction of the ultimate reality—consisting of the mutual conjunction of these [cognitions]?
If Maheśvara were not the one who has internalized the infinite universal form,
he would not be the singular embodiment of consciousness possessing the power to know and to remove forgetfulness.
IPV: Consciousness itself is the universal form, because nothing other than it is logically possible;
it is the mutual synthesis of the cognitions of all objects.
Its very powers are those of cognition and so forth.
"For from Me come memory, knowledge, and their absence," so it has been said.
Thus ends the third chapter in the section on knowledge.
For he, being one who has previously perceived an object and existing even at a later time, reflects "that is it" and, being independent, is designated as "one who remembers. (IPK 1.4.1)
Even subsequently, because [the subject] remains the experiencer of the object previously experienced, there is no loss of the manifestation of that previously experienced object;
rather, the activity called "memory" consists in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of that single, all-pervading agent as "this is *that*" by way of its having been previously experienced.

And at its own time, it should illuminate [the object], while reflecting upon what was previously illuminated—either as a mere appearance of the jar in its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or in its entirety. (IPK 1.4.2)

IPV: By the power of memory (*smṛtiśakti*), [the subject], while referring (*parāmṛśan*) to that previously experienced particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as "that," necessarily causes it to appear; otherwise, no reflection (*parāmarśa*) of what has been manifested would have occurred. And since this occurs at the very time of its own existence, there is no fault in its appearance even though it has perished at the time of recollection. However, sometimes, due to the force of desire (*arthitā*), its clear manifestation occurs in the form of a single appearance among others, such as the jar, the substance gold, or the existence [of the object].
But at other times, through a state of seeking with one's whole being, it is exactly the same;
however, for one whose mind is exceptionally and continuously attentive, there is indeed the direct perception of the object already seen.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the object being remembered should appear if there were a difference [between the memory and the original experience];
therefore, there is oneness [of the object] across cognitions occurring at different times, and this is the Knower.

IPV: Furthermore, an object previously experienced, appearing in the manifestation of a simultaneous recollection along with that experience, is indeed non-different from the recollection; for it is logically impossible for that which is distinct from the manifestation to be manifest.
Thus, there is a unity among cognitions such as experience, recollection, and so forth, and that very unity is the self, the knower. For instance:
For the prior experience does not appear in memory as something separate from the object, like the object itself;
this is because [memory] appears as having ascended upon the self in the form "I previously experienced."

In memory (smṛti), the experienced object being remembered appears as something separate; however, the experience itself does not appear in that same way, because it manifests as consisting of experience itself within the very self, which is cognized as "I-ness" (ahaṃtā).
Furthermore, that object which is known as "I" throughout multiple moments of time is precisely the Self (ātman).
Even for yogins, these [perceptions] do not appear as objects of sight in another vision;
they shine either as having self-awareness alone as their sole means of knowledge, or even in the domain of the object of cognition.

IPV: Even for the omniscient ones, the perceptions residing in other cognizers would appear as being mounted solely upon their own self, having a nature that is knowable by their own self-consciousness alone;
therefore, for those yogins, the very reality is the attainment of the state of another's self.
Even at the level of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), they would appear in their own individual form as pure consciousness, like a jar or other objects, if such were possible.

When one remembers, "That very vision which was mine [in the past] is thus," even through such differentiation, that is indeed the grammatical analysis (vyākaraṇa) of this memory, because of the recollection: "It was seen by me. (IPK 1.4.6)
IPV: "It was seen by me" is a distinct statement consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the act of seeing inherent within the subject;
this very same [act] is also indicated through differentiation as "this experience of mine occurred thus.
And there is also the resolution: "I see this," or "this is a jar."
She too considers that perception to be inherent in the perceiver.

Even when conceptualizing an object situated externally, the perception—whether expressed as "I see this jar" or "this is a jar"—is reflected upon as being essentially constituted by the subject alone.
"That is seen by me," "this one has been seen by me"—even while reflecting thus, two objects, non-different from the states of subject and object, appear within the cognizer. (IPK 1.4.8)
Therefore, in memory— which is preceded by the reflective awareness of perception— or even in mere conceptual thought, even without the interpenetration of the word "perception" (dṛk),

when there is a reference to the object alone as "that" or "this," both the perceived object and the perceiver appear everywhere as dissolved within the single subject, even though they manifest as separated by the power of Māyā.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Section on Knowledge.
The manifestation of entities appearing as present occurs only for those situated within [consciousness], even though they appear as external objects.
Even in the case of perception, it is logical that the appearance of objects as distinct occurs only while they remain dissolved within the cognizer.
As before, the object would be unmanifest without the nature of manifestation;
nor could the manifestation of the object's self-nature be something distinct from that manifestation itself.
IPV: Without having the nature of light designated as the cognizer, just as a jar would not appear to him at the outset, so it would also be at the time of cognition;
moreover, the manifestation of an object is its very nature as light, and not something distinct from it.
If manifestation were divided while the manifestor remained undivided, there would be a confusion of objects;
for an object is established as manifest only when it is of the nature of manifestation, not when it is non-manifest.

If light were distinct from objects and common to all objects, then the restriction of the object—such that "this is the illumination of this jar" and "this is [the illumination] of this cloth alone"—would be without foundation.
Therefore, the establishment of an object depends upon its having the nature of light.
If that various spontaneous appearance were to cause the inference of an external object, it would not be so;
for a consciousness that is non-different [from its objects] cannot be the cause of diverse appearances.
For insentient things, existence is established solely through their appearing; and that appearance is nothing other than having manifestation as its very nature.
Consequently, pure consciousness alone is the single reality here.

Although it is without distinction, the gradual differentiation of the manifestation of objects leads one to infer an external object—distinct from that [consciousness] and not itself manifesting—as the cause, just like a sense organ.
Nor can a diverse awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) serve as the cause here; for what would be the basis for the diversity of that very awakening? (IPK 1.5.5)
Objection: The awakening of diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not distinct from consciousness;
what, then, is the cause of that diversity?
Therefore, it is only an external object that serves as the cause for the appearance of differentiation.
It might be argued: "Since all worldly transaction is concluded within those very appearances themselves, what is the use of another external object that is logically untenable?"
IPV: Since linguistic and practical activity proceeds by means of objects merely as appearances, let those appearances themselves be the essence; what loss is there?
What need is there for an external object, since the course of worldly life is accomplished by that much alone?

Furthermore, an external object is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for if it were composed of parts, it would be contradicted by the superimposition of contradictory properties and so forth, and if it were partless, it would be contradicted by its connection with six spatial directions and other such arguments, as has been shown many times.
For the Lord, whose very self is consciousness, manifests the entire range of objects externally from within, by the power of His will, without any material cause, just as a yogi does. 1.5.7

IPV: Consciousness itself, because it is the Lord, manifests as its own essential nature; and by virtue of its infinite power, through the force of its will, it may manifest the entire mass of objects—such as pots, cloths, and so forth—as external, even without causes such as clay.

Inference is not accepted [as a means of knowing] that which has never appeared before; nor is it [the case for] the sense organ, since the causal entity, such as a seed, is indeed already manifested through its appearance. (IPK 1.5.8)

IPV: Inference (*anumāna*) is the reflective discernment (*vimarśana*) regarding an object already present within prior manifestation, which—by virtue of perceiving an invariably concomitant object—is joined with its respective place, time, and so forth.
Even a sense organ (*indriya*) is inferred; it is a certain minimal cause, and that [cause] is indeed manifested through the appearance of seeds and the like.
Furthermore, how could an appearance ever belong to an external object? Therefore, its existence is established neither through perception nor through inference.
IPV: Since an external object corresponding to the appearance of a jar and so forth is logically untenable, that appearance did not exist [externally];
therefore, its establishment does not occur even through inference.
The manifestation of the multitude of entities established within the Self belongs to the Lord alone;
indeed, without that [manifestation], the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of will does not proceed. (IPK 1.5.10)

Indeed, because the Lord is non-different from his own Self, even with respect to objects that appear [as external], there would not otherwise exist a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—which consists of will and whose nature is that of a creator—having as its sole object the thing appearing in another way. They know reflective awareness to be the very essence of manifestation; otherwise, even if it were colored by an object, manifestation would be like an insentient crystal or similar substance. (IPK 1.5.11)

IPV: The primary essence of light is self-reflection (*pratyavamarśa*); without that, even though it possesses a form differentiated by objects, it would have mere transparency but no consciousness, because there would be an absence of wonder (*camatkṛti*).
Therefore, consciousness itself is the self; it is the activity of consciousness and the agency of consciousness.
It is for this reason that it has been described as having this essential nature, for it is indeed distinct from the insentient.

IPV: Although this nature of the self-substance is of the nature of existence (*bhāva*), it is said to be its primary form, called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which distinguishes it from the insentient; it is consciousness (*caitanya*), the power of seeing (*dṛśi-śakti*), and cognition (*citi*).
That activity of consciousness is precisely the agency of cognition itself.
Consciousness, whose nature is self-reflective awareness, is the supreme speech arising from its own inherent savor;
this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self.

IPV: This speech, whose denotative content and other attributes are non-different [from consciousness], is by its nature eternal consciousness; it is without beginning or end and is not dependent on anything else.
This purity, independent of any other entity, is called sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
That throbbing Great Being, which is undifferentiated by space or time, is declared to be the very essence; it is the Heart of the Supreme Lord.

IPV: The state of being manifest (*sphuradrūpatā*) is the agency of manifestation; it is existence (*sattā*) which does not have non-existence as its counter-correlative and which pervades all non-existence; it is the state of being (*bhavattā*), the agency of becoming (*bhavanakartṛtā*), which is eternal because it is untouched by space and time. That very [existence] is the power of the activity of consciousness whose essence is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). That [power], being the form of the Supreme Lord’s own self-abiding within the Universal Self (*viśvātman*), is called "the Heart" (*hṛdaya*) in various scriptures.

For this very reason, he may make the self an object of knowledge while it remains in a state of separation; however, because of its orientation toward that object of knowledge, his sovereignty is not fragmented. (IPK 1.5.15)

IPV: By virtue of such pure sovereignty, he does not perceive this object as something established separately; rather, through his unimpeded power, he makes the unknowable Self into an object of knowledge. If there were dependence on a separate object of knowledge, the agency of knowing would wither away.

The Lord, through his absolute sovereignty, having fashioned from his non-dual nature a self that is liberated by that very sovereignty, employs it in worldly transaction by means of volitions such as those of Īśvara and others.

Therefore, by virtue of that very sovereignty consisting of fullness— characterized by the unification with the object of knowledge— the Lord Śiva causes the self, which is the knower at that very moment, to appear through such conceptual constructions as "I am the knower" or "Śiva is the knower," for the sake of practical activities such as meditation and the like.
Because this [universe], which is not distinct from the Self, does not differ from the reflection of "I" and so forth,
it exists solely as the object of the "I-reflection," just like the object expressed by a verbal suffix.
In the state of the present subject, the "this-ness" (*idantā*) of the reflective awareness of "I" does not exist as an object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore,

when there is a difference in reflection (*vimarśa*) and a difference in manifestation (*ābhāsa*), it is the subject alone who is designated by the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), being merely [the self] through the mediation of the reflective awareness of "I," just as the meaning expressed by words such as "cooking" (*pacati*) is [designated] by words such as "action" (*kriyā*).

As they have said: actions, qualities, universals, relations, and so forth, are not denoted by words such as "action" and the like, because they are expressed through the medium of [verbs] such as "he cooks.
Likewise, when one reflects upon the self with the word "Lord" or the word "Self," one does not know the self directly;
yet there is indeed a cognition, just as there is a recollection of what was previously experienced through the medium of that experience.

That very power of Māyā belonging to the All-pervasive Lord, when its sphere of objects becomes differentiated, is designated by such names as knowledge (jñāna), volition (saṃkalpa), and determination (adhyavasāya). (IPK 1.5.18)
IPV: By the power of *māyā*, the universe—which is the very form of His own self—is manifested as differentiated by the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light.
Therefore, that very consciousness (*cit*) is knowledge and direct perception.

Furthermore, even when it takes the form of the mind and intellect—namely, memory, volition, and determination regarding that same [universe] which appears as differentiated—it is indeed consciousness alone.

Even at the moment of direct perception, there must be reflective awareness; otherwise, how could activities such as running be possible without the synthesis [of prior and subsequent cognitions]? (IPK 1.5.19)
Even in a cognition characterized by direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), there exists a subtle reflective awareness of the object on the part of consciousness;
for swift action in speech, running, and so forth, must indeed arise through the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of the desire to acquire or avoid those respective perceived objects, places, and so on.
The determination "this is a jar" is not something distinct from name and form; rather, it is the power of the Supreme Lord appearing like the Self, and not as an objectified "this-ness."

IPV: This determinative cognition, such as "this" or "pot," appears non-differently as consisting solely of the power of consciousness (*citiśaktimaya*), like the Self itself, transcending the name and form that appear as distinct.
It is solely due to the influence of different objects of cognition in terms of space and time that knowledge, memory, determination, and so forth appear as if they possess a temporal sequence.

IPV: By the power of Māyā, the object of consciousness—such as a jar and so forth—which is differentiated from the *cittattva* (the essence of consciousness), is manifested as distinct according to its respective place and time; because it is supported by non-difference from that [consciousness], cognition, memory, and so forth appear as if they were divided by space, time, and other such factors.
Thus ends the fifth chapter (*āhnika*) in the Section on Knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*).
That reflective awareness which, though its nature is light and consists of speech, is not a conceptual construction;
for that is said to be a conceptual construction which, being a determination, implies a duality.

IPV: Because light, in its own self, consists of the nature of *parāvāk* as "I," even that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) which is accompanied by verbal expression is said not to be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for while a conceptual construction is a determination preceded by the negation of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), no such counter-correlate is possible here.
For there may indeed be an appearance of two distinct things, such as a jar and a non-jar;
however, there is no manifestation of anything else that is separate from the Light itself.
IPV: If a second, distinct counter-correlate (pratiyogin) termed "non-manifestation" were not perceived alongside manifestation, then there would be no such thing as being "other than manifestation.
Since its exclusion is impossible without its appearance, the status of conceptual construction (vikalpatā) would be lost.
And thus,

by the mere exclusion of what is not that [object], through the manifestation of that and its opposite, this conceptual construction "this is a jar" is said to be the ascertainment of that object. (IPK 1.6.3)

IPV: The activity called conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the ascertainment "this is a jar" through the exclusion of what it is not, belonging to the cognizer himself, who is independent and in whom the appearances of both that object and its opposite are internally latent.
Having abandoned the true nature of consciousness through illusion, that which appears as if divided—
whether in the body, in the intellect, or in the vital breath— is like [the appearance of division] in the sky.
The reflective awareness "I" as the subject of cognition arises through the exclusion of others; it is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by the manifestation of its opposite.

In the Vivaraṇa: For the Lord, whose very nature is consciousness, when a body appears as differentiated through the power of *māyā*—whether internally within the intellect or externally as a tactile object—or when that which transcends these is conceptualized as "I" like the void of space, there occurs a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of the subject. Because this performs the exclusion (*apohana*) of the various counter-correlates such as the appearing body and so forth, it is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), just like the thought "this is a jar."

The conceptual construction (kalpanā) that occurs when there is an occasional manifestation, which joins it with a previous manifestation and so forth, is said to arise from mental impressions (saṃskāra); and that too [is conceptual] even when the manifestation is distinct.

IPV: Among the various distinct appearances of the void, the body, and so forth, that which consists of the unification of the previous appearances—namely those called "I" and "ego"—and which rests upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the persistence of those previous appearances, is indeed *kalpanā* (conceptual construction) in the form of the subject's activity;
this is what is termed recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Thus, even in the realm of empirical transaction, the Lord, entering the body and so forth,
may by His will manifest externally the multitude of objects that are already shining within.

IPV: Whether at the time of the initial creation or even in ordinary worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), Maheśvara, by means of his power of *māyā*, identifies with the body and so forth as the self, making them the subject (*pramātṛ*).
He then causes each respective object, which is already situated within and shining [there], to appear externally in succession through his power of agency (*kartṛśakti*).
Such an appearance is itself what constitutes "production" (*utpādana*).
But for this [Self], which is not entered by the body and so forth, there is by its own nature the simultaneous manifestation of all objects in the form "I am this."
Thus, whether in memory, or in conceptualization which is intent on exclusion (apohana), or even in cognition, it is certain that an internal appearance remains present. (IPK 1.6.8)
IPV: In all cognitions, the manifestation of all objects, merged within the subject, remains ever-present, shining forth in conformity with the nature of consciousness (cittattva).
However, while the innate nature of cognition consists in appearing as something external,
that which has the form of a prior experience persists in memory and other such mental states.
In the case of cognition whose nature is the manifestation of an external object, the internal appearance of the object is indeed innate to the *cittattva* (the essence of consciousness);
however, in memory and similar states, it consists of a previous experience.
For this very reason, memory is said to arise from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
This [power] exists naturally within conceptual construction as it moves at its own will,
because it causes the appearance of forms according to one's intention within the domain of the intellect.

However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), though independent, brings even that which is not within the range of the eyes and other senses into the domain of the Buddha; by presenting each respective object as something entirely new—without reflecting on its having been previously experienced—it manifests according to one's inclination both the object itself and its specific configuration (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*).
In this regard, that object exists as something innate (*sahaja*).
Therefore, because the manifestation of whatever is intended appears [within it], both knowledge and action are clearly established for every living being. (IPK 1.6.11)
IPV: And because of the power of the knowledge that creates objects never before perceived, it is clear that for everyone, omniscience and omnipotence reside in conceptual thought alone.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Section on Knowledge;
[now begins] the seventh chapter.

And that intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), which is colored by the sequence of various objects, is the cognizer whose nature is non-sequential and infinite consciousness; he is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). (IPK 1.7.1)

Moreover, this very subject known as the Self—consisting of infinite consciousness and pervading the succession of all cognitions and times—is permeated by the sequence of various objects; while remaining internal, it is the manifestor, and as the creator with respect to the object of knowledge which has become its own limb, it is the Great Lord.
When entities, through the various gateways of their distinct cognitions, become established within a single subject,
this state of being known (jñāteya) comes into being.

Indeed, by merging into the single ocean of the cognizer through the various mouths of the streams of manifold consciousnesses, the distinctions between entities attain a coherent integration within the conventional discourse of cause and effect and so forth.
This [synthesis] is to be accomplished by the simultaneous appearance of objects that possess a sequence of space and time and are self-contained; otherwise, what kind of synthesis could there be?
The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and the manifestation (*avabhāsana*) of entities are established solely within their own self. Their unification is based on their simultaneous appearance as one;
that [unification] is conceived as non-different because it is dissolved into the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
The establishment of the causal relationship between perceptions and non-perceptions— which fall upon their respective distinct aspects—
is due to their arising from a single cognizing subject.

Just as the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), its establishment is also brought about through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) by way of a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*), having attained a state of concomitance (*samanvaya*).
Perception and non-perception that are not thus concomitant are exhausted in merely making known their own respective sequential objects; they are incapable of characterizing a mutual dependence.

In the case of memory, that very self-awareness which serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of its own nature is itself the proof for the existence of the prior experience, and nothing else.

IPV: Because there is no self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of a prior experience, it is precisely the self-awareness of the memory that serves as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) here, appearing as a single object and having the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), just like the nature of the memory itself.
Since the causal relationship cannot be established in the absence of the appearance of the prior experience for the memory, it does not function as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) based on an effect.
The relationship between the sublated and the sublator also arises among cognitions that are opposed to their own self-abiding,
because they are all ultimately grounded in a single knowing subject.
IPV: What contradiction can there be between cognitions that rest solely upon their own distinct appearances?
How, then, could there be the relationship of the sublated and the sublator?
This [relationship] is logical only when [cognitions] find repose in a single subject (*pramātṛ*).
Just as the cognition of a bare ground is the knowledge of the absence of a jar, so too the cognition of mother-of-pearl is the knowledge of the invalidity of the cognition of silver. (IPK 1.7.7)

For example: "There is no jar on this ground"—the cognition of the absence of the jar is simply the cognition of the bare ground, because the empty ground is itself the nature of the absence of the jar.

In the same way, if it is argued that because shell and silver are not identical to one another, the cognition of the shell is the non-cognition of the silver, then perception would be the sublater [of the illusion].
The absence of that [object] in its nature as a jar would not be established by the cognition of a pure location in this way;
for even though it is capable of being perceived, there is no absence here of its nature as a jar.

IPV: From the cognition of the bare ground alone, it is established that the ground has the nature of being without a jar; however, this does not mean that there is no distinct jar present in that locus which is capable of being perceived.
The ground of reality is eternally secluded because all entities are established within their own nature;
how, then, could knowledge of that [ground] ever establish a separate non-existence?
[Objection: The ground is always distinct from the absence of a jar; how then could the cognition of it establish the absence of a separate jar only at certain times?

Furthermore, what would be the nature of the ground’s state of being distinct from a separate jar at any time, if its nature were also sometimes its state of being accompanied by a jar? But this is not the case.
Both entities are established solely within their own respective natures.
That [cognition] which consists of both [the object and its absence] is not something distinct from the literary composition (sāhitya), but is a single form of knowledge;
for although it consists of the conjunction of the appearances of both, it takes the form of the absence of any other cognition possessing the appearance of one [of those two].

Furthermore, since a real entity (vastu) determines itself as being restricted to its own locus, the establishment of the absence of a jar does not occur through the force of the real entity in the same way that the establishment of a location occurs from the perception of that location.
However, [the cognition] could exist because its effect consists of a single cognition in which both [the object and the sense organ] appear;
yet it is not so, for there is no perception through mediation, since that [object] is established merely by seeing the location.
However, for one who is blind, there exists a mass of light, or a soft touch such as heat and so forth;
by means of that, one may establish his own cognition of the jar's non-existence.

In the case of locations, after perceiving light in the dark, or a soft, warm, and so forth, tactile sensation—which consists in the absence of the color and touch of a jar—one is justified in employing the conventional expressions: "the absence of a jar exists here" or "the jar is not here."
Just as a *piśāca* might exist within the light even though it is not visible, so too the end of the earth is invisible; it cannot be denied in any way.
And it is not the case that, because light is different from a *piśāca*, there would follow the undesirable consequence of negating a *piśāca* therein;
for that [the *piśāca*] is invisible, and even though it is different, just as it cannot be excluded from within a lump of clay, so too it cannot be excluded from within the light.
Therefore, just as in the opinion of others, in our view as well, its non-existence is not established on the grounds of its invisibility.
In this way, the cognition of mother-of-pearl would consist in the absence of the manifestation of silver;
however, it would not be the indicator of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver. (IPK 1.7.12)

IPV: It is established that the very cognition of mother-of-pearl is of the nature of the absence of the cognition of silver; therefore, the invalidity of the past cognition of silver—which is distinct from the experience of the present cognition of mother-of-pearl—is not [established].
Even if the property [of the subject] were unestablished, there would be no sublation by means of inference;
rather, it is logical that [the cognition] established through self-awareness arises from a single cognizer.
IPV: Furthermore, at the time of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, the prior cognition of silver does not exist;
therefore, since that subject (*dharmin*) is not established, there can be no sublation by means of inference.
However, in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which consists of a single cognizing subject, it is established because the relation consisting of both cognitions appears as resting upon a single locus.

Subsequent corroboration occurs in the case of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) because even the preceding [cognition] appears therein; thus, one becomes a valid means of knowledge while the other is otherwise.
Furthermore, this corroboration is produced by a single cognizer.
Thus, within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the appearance of objects that are extremely diverse,
worldly transaction— whether defiled or stainless— is experienced.

IPV: Through the power of *māyā*, this entire worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) has as its object differentiation; likewise, through ignorance, it appears pure to those who are not blinded by ignorance, but as impure to those who are. This is possible because the Blessed One possesses the manifestation of various distinct objects, as established by direct experience.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the section on knowledge.
Appearances depend solely upon the immediate perception of the senses in some cases;
otherwise, in other instances, such as in blindness or dense darkness, they do not. (IPK 1.8.1)

IPV: Sometimes appearances are projected by immediate perception and serve as the cause for the conventional usage "this is a jar," whereas in cases such as pitch darkness, they arise from prior experience.
There is no distinction whatsoever in the existence of the appearance of an object within conceptual constructions that refer to objects yet to be, currently being, or already past.

In conceptual constructions (vikalpa) consisting of memory or imagination—whether they follow upon direct perception or are independent, and whether their objects belong to the three times—the appearance of the object remains situated equally within [the mind].
And regarding pleasure and so forth, as well as the objects that are the causes of pleasure and so forth,
even though their appearance exists, they remain as such because they have passed away.

Even though the appearances of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the appearances of their means, always exist internally, they do not produce a state consisting of that joy and so on, because they have passed away and are absent externally at that time; for it is only those things characterized by their presence at that very moment that act in such a way.
But when pleasure and so forth are intensely delineated by conceptual construction, their state remains exactly as it was, because they are clearly perceived in that very way. (IPK 1.8.4)
IPV: From the application of some effort, pleasure and so forth—clearly produced by independent conceptualization—arise as the cause of expansion and so on.
For appearances of existence and non-existence, externality is held to be the limiting condition;
their essence is not their being, since they are always internal existents.

IPV: Although all appearances—whether having existence or non-existence as their object—are not external in nature, they nonetheless possess existence in memory and so forth; for externality is merely an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) of these appearances and not their essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Even in the case of the appearance of non-existence, its status as such is due to its absence externally despite its internal existence.

Because they are internal, when there is identity with the cognizer, there is no purposeful action (arthakriyā) based on their difference; even when they are external, that action is [determined] by the difference in their distinct appearances.

And even though all manifestations, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, always exist within [the subject], because they consist solely of the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) based on distinctions such as cause and effect.

Even when the cognizer is differentiated, the causal efficacy residing in the manifestations also differs according to the differentiation of the manifestations—such as being mental or visual—with respect to form and so forth.
Insofar as appearances consist of consciousness, their abiding is always only within;
yet for those appearing through māyā, because of their externality, that abiding exists even outside.
IPV: Because they are of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), appearances always abide within the inner reality itself.
When objects—which are non-different from the Light—are manifested externally through the power of *māyā* as if they were perceptible, this is called their "external appearance.
Yet even that is merely their internality; this is also the case for objects at the time of the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*) and so forth.
Even this mental representation within conceptual thought appears as something external and distinct;
internal unity consists in its identity with the subject, whereas externality is indeed its differentiation from that.

In the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even when there is no mention of a jar or the like within the range of the eyes and other senses, it appears as something distinct and is therefore indeed external.
For the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*) constitutes internality, whereas the awareness of "this" (*idam*) constitutes externality.

And thus, for objects such as jars, there is a twofold externality— namely, being cognizable by both the external and internal organs— whereas for pleasure and the like, there is only the state of being cognizable by the internal organ alone.
The manifestation of the mental impression (*ullekha*) and of pleasure and so forth occurs externally,
by the will of the Lord, in the form of direct perception (*adhyakṣarūpa*), just as [the manifestation] of those things arising from the senses and so forth does.

IPV: Just as there is a mental manifestation (*bauddha-prakāśa*) consisting of direct perception through the power of the Lord regarding visible things such as color and so forth, as well as mention, pleasure, pain, shame, and the like; [so it is here].
Without that unity, the worldly course of cognitions would not exist;
because of the unity of light, that oneness is established as "the subject is one. (IPK 1.8.10)
IPV: For worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) occurs through the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of those various distinct cognitions (*saṃvit*).
And that which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) is one, consisting of that very synthesis; and that alone is the single subject (*pramātṛ*), known as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
He alone, through his constant nature as reflective awareness, is Maheśvara;
for the pure knowledge and action of the Lord consist of nothing other than this very awareness.
That Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) by virtue of His primary and unerring essential nature called *vimarśa*.

For the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), which is the self of the universe and designated as Śiva, the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśana*) alone constitutes pure knowledge and action;
however, when these relate to objects of knowledge and effects that are both distinct and non-distinct [from Him], they belong to Īśvara and are thus both pure and impure.

But with respect to objects of differentiated meaning, for a person, the functions of *sattva* and *rajas*—known as illumination (*prakāśa*) and activity (*pravṛtti*)—are merely impure when they are contracted by *tamas*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the section on Knowledge.
Thus ends the chapter on Knowledge. Now begins the chapter on Action.
The First Daily Lesson.
Therefore, even that which was stated—that action cannot be successive for a single [agent] because it is one, and so forth—is refuted by the establishment of the oneness [of the agent]. (IPK 2.1.1)

IPV: Since the unity of the mental substance (*cittatva*) is established, the operation belonging to that single [substance] is indeed one; thus, the objection against the action (*kriyā*) is also refuted.

And the sequential nature of worldly action is possible through the power of time, but it is not so for that which is eternal; rather, it belongs to the sovereign power of the Lord, as is the case with the Lord himself.

IPV: And the activity of the appearances of differentiated entities, which arise from the power of *māyā*, is sequential due to the influence of the power of time (*kāla-śakti*); however, it is not the [activity] of the Lord, which consists of self-reflection (*ātma-vimarśa*), is without beginning or end, and is His very nature.
Time is the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, or the blooming of various flowers and the like;
or rather, it is characterized by cold and heat—in reality, it is simply that sequence. (IPK 2.1.3)

IPV: That well-known action, or time characterized by cold and so forth—which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for all appearing entities that manifest as distinct—or rather, it is succession itself, because it is precisely that which is useful for [the manifestation of] those [entities].
Succession is based on differentiation; differentiation, too, arises from the presence or absence of manifestation.
The presence or absence of manifestation, however, is produced by the Lord through His manifold manifestations.
IPV: The very activity of the manifold appearance of distinct entities, which are empty of mutual reflection, is the cause of succession within the Lord's manifestations.
Through the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests the succession of space;
through the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He also manifests the succession of time. (IPK 2.1.5)
In the case of multiple [entities], there is a sequence of space due to the appearance of mutual differentiation, and there is also a sequence of time by way of action.
However, for a single entity, there is only a sequence of time due to the differentiation of actions such as its successive births, existence, transformation, and so forth.
Everywhere there would also be a difference in manifestation, taking the form of temporal succession;
for the manifestation of the void and so forth is fragmented, whereas that of the Mother [the subject] is not simultaneous.
In every object, the manifold appearance is the cause for the appearance of temporal succession for the subject whose body and so forth are empty;

for that [past] time does not appear at that moment in the same way [as it did before], except through memory. And it is in relation to its own present that one employs the conventions of "past" and "future.

However, because there is no interruption in the act of manifestation for that which has manifested all at once, and because there is an absence of counting repetitions, there is no differentiation of time even with respect to objects, just as there is none with respect to the Self.

Even the sequence of space appears among objects to the limited self of the Mother; but to the Unlimited One, all objects appear as full within His own Self, by His own Self, as if they were His very own essence.
With respect to a limited cognizer (*pramātṛ*), entities are distinct from one another and possess designations such as "far" and so forth;
however, for the Lord (*īśvara*), whose sole nature is light, there is no possibility of non-manifestation anywhere—not even in the case of atoms.
For that which is a mass of light, nothing appears as separate from itself, nor as distant, nor as distinct from anything else.
However, that power of manifestation also belongs to the Lord who knows thus;
for it is by Him that the distinction between the knower and the knowable is made manifest.

IPV: Even though the Supreme Lord shines forth in this way in His fullness, this very power of creation is that by which entities—whose nature consists of the knower and the known—are perceived as distinct from themselves and from one another; yet, through such perception, His abiding in His own essential nature is not concealed.
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on action.
The second chapter.
The cognitions of action, relation, generality, substance, space, and time are real;
they are considered to have both single and multiple substrata due to their stability and utility. (IPK 2.2.1)
Objection: Other relations and so forth, such as action, though they may have both single and multiple objects, are also appearances of reality;
for these, which are useful at all times, cannot be discarded because they possess functional efficacy (*arthavattva*).
In that regard, there is one internal reality which, having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses,
becomes manifold through [differences of] place, time, and intrinsic nature.
IPV: Reality itself is indeed non-different; it is both one and many due to the difference in internal and external manifestations.

Each individual manifestation consists of a confluence of differences in external space, time, and intrinsic nature, because the manifestations of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are manifold.

Taking those two as its object, this mind, acting as a subsequent reflective awareness, performs the conceptual constructions of action and so forth, consisting of the activity of the subject. (IPK 2.2.3)

IPV: By virtue of being situated in the middle, the mental constructions regarding the categories of internal and external reality—such as action and so forth—are of the nature of the subject's activity.

Entities, which are distinct appearances grounded in their own selves, become the locus of the cognition of relation when they are joined with a unity consisting of mutual interpenetration within a single subject. (IPK 2.2.4)

In such cases as "the king's man," the cognition of a relation, because its internal synthesis is unitary, takes on both unity and the external distinction between the relata as its objective support.

Conceptual constructions take as their objective support both the uniformity of universals and substances even when they appear externally, as well as the distinction between the individual instance and its parts.

Moreover, cognitions such as "cows" and "Caitra," even when directed toward external objects, reflect both the unity of the appearance of the mere cow or the specific individual man as a single solid mass, and the multiplicity of the appearances of the parts of their respective particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The coordination of the factors of action (kārakas) has as its object the deliberation regarding the activity;
the cognition of direction and so forth is based on the relation between the limit and that which is limited.

Vṛtti: In the case of "he cooks the wood, the ground, Devadatta, and the rice," because of internal connection and external distinction, there arises a cognition of action directed toward both the one and the many.

Furthermore, the temporal sequence of entities—which consist of the nature of the limit (the object) and that which has limits (the agent)—is merely a specific relation based on mutual dependence, and it is likewise composed of the one and the many.
All cognitions of genus, substance, action, number, and so forth, have as their object only the inherence (*samavāya*) within specific relations.
In this very way, the accomplishment of the mother’s purpose would occur for one who seeks effective action;
therefore, such an error does not exist by virtue of an object that possesses both difference and non-difference.

IPV: It is precisely through actions and so forth, which possess both unitary and manifold forms, that there occurs for the cognizer seeking that object a correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in accordance with such appearances;
therefore, those cognitions are not erroneous.
Thus ends the second chapter in the section on action.
The third daily lesson.
That by virtue of which an object is determined as "this is such-and-such" is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it too is a self-manifestation that arises afresh.

Thus, that cognition whose nature consists in internal reflection is an uncontradicted means of knowledge regarding an object that is the referent of a single designation, even though it is undivided by space, time, and other such factors.

For when the state of being established— whether by the essential nature of an object or by its qualifiers— is dependent [on the subject], that [state] exists as a manifestation of a new object for the cognizer by virtue of its own right, and thus it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And that very manifestation, having ascended into the cognizer as "this" or "eternal," and having attained the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) precisely through its distinctness and novelty, becomes expressed by individual words according to the specific differences of that reflective awareness, each being indeed separate.

When that object, whose distinctions such as place and so forth have been set aside, appears in its universal form and accomplishes its own causal function, the resulting cognition— whose stability remains uncontradicted by any other means of valid knowledge— is the activity of the cognizer.
Even when a single object is established through synthesis, its appearance varies according to one's inclination, one's purpose, and one's proficiency. (IPK 2.3.3)

Moreover, even with respect to a single entity—which is established by the capacity for a single unifying reflective awareness—there occurs a differentiation of appearances either by the force of one's own will, in accordance with practical needs, or by the force of technical expertise.
For instance,
by means of [attributes] such as being long, round, upright, a person, smoke, or the nature of firewood, appearances—
which are not differentiated by space or time— are distinguished according to their respective manifestations.
In the same way, the various appearances—such as the substance of a clay pot, its golden luster, and so forth—which produce distinct effects, are the referents of words. (IPK 2.3.5)
For instance, in the case of a single object such as a jar, depending on one's interest (*avadhitsā*), its length, triangularity, sphericity, or other qualities may appear;

or, when there is a desire for merely the shadow cast by the obstruction of a mark, only the verticality of the man appears; but when there is a desire for his specific function, the man appears in his full detail (*nyakṣeṇa*) to one who observes him closely.
To some, only smoke appears; but to one who knows it, its nature as grass-fire and so forth appears, just as the specific qualities of a gem or silver appear [to an expert].
And although it is thus differentiated, it does not touch upon any difference of place or time.

In the same way, the jar itself, while being real, appears as eternal; it is entirely distinct from cloth and all other infinite objects, yet it performs causal functions such as the conceptualization of existence—which is established by mere being—and so forth.

Within that very [jar], the appearance "this is a jar" is something known through internal and external senses, consisting of the general form of the object with its broad base and belly, which is different from what exists in cloth and the like.

Furthermore, there is another [appearance], namely "golden," which does not exist in earthenware and the like; and that too arises as a sensory perception precisely due to the force of such a desire or need.
Each of these appearances is designated by a single word for the sake of conventional usage by those who require its respective specific causal efficiency; thus,
it is called "jar," and neither "existence" nor "gold" is used to designate the appearance of a jar.
"Caitra" is common to [the states of] childhood and so forth, and likewise devoid of place and other such attributes;
therefore, its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is distinct [from that of others].
Furthermore, the restricted causal efficiency of things arises from the difference in their appearances;
for those that appear as non-different, this occurs through their appearing in a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

In the Individual (Ipv): Within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the effect is determined by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) for each respective manifestation; thus, it is both the substratum of various manifestations that produce such manifold effects and yet remains one.
It is a "thing" (*vastu*) by virtue of the manifestation of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for co-referentiality is indeed the oneness of the manifold.
Just as the lights of separate lamps or the currents of rivers in the ocean have non-contradictory appearances yet perform a single function, so too is the cognition of unity.
Just as distinct lamp-lights appear without division, as do the currents of rivers in the cognition of the ocean, and various tastes in a *pānaka* drink;
likewise, the appearances of whiteness, largeness, cloth-ness, and so forth, are capable of mutual interpenetration.
However, the appearances of blue, yellow, and so on, are not conceived—even in direct perception—as having the nature of a single substance or a single effect, such as those [other] appearances.
This is what constitutes grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
In that regard, with respect to fire and so forth which are undifferentiated, their status as cause and effect, their heat,
and their nature as the referents of their respective words are understood from a single means of valid cognition.

IPV: At some point, by abandoning the particularity of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) delimited by coexistence with place and other factors, there arises— through a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone— the establishment of the nature of being denotable by the word "fire" and so forth, such as being a specific cause and effect and having an upward-moving heat, based solely on the appearance of fire as a single universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) that pervades the three worlds and the three times.

However, even for one who desires [an object], their activity regarding a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is distinct from other particulars such as place and so forth—would have to be based on inference at that very moment. (IPK 2.3.9)

Furthermore, activity regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself arises from a collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), accompanied by the distinctions of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding place, time, and so forth, because of the desire for that [object].
Even from inference, activity occurs only when it is qualified by the direct perception of the locus (*dharmī*).

By means of the distance or proximity of objects, by their being unperceived or perceived, by their being external or internal, by defects, or otherwise through the nature of the manifestor. (IPK 2.3.10)
Even for those whose appearances and shadows are distinct, unity is not precluded by virtue of the primary appearance known as the single reflective awareness (ekapratyavamarśa). (IPK 2.3.11)

IPV: Even though there is a difference in the mere shadow (*chāyāmātra*) of the manifestation—due to being distant or near, clear or unclear, or moving externally or internally—the unity of objects remains uncontradicted because of the identity of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) which constitutes their primary essential nature.
Even the causal efficiency of things is innate and not determined by the will of a Lord;
for that [efficiency] is fixed by Him, and thus its non-activity could not be anything other than [the absence of] activity.

IPV: Although images such as jars lack external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), they appear precisely as jars and so forth; for that [efficiency], which is not inherent to them, has been regulated by the Lord according to each individual manifestation.
Even when there is a single reflective awareness of silver, silver does not exist in the mother-of-pearl shell;
because the location of the limiting adjunct does not correspond [to the object], as in the case of the double moon, the sky appears otherwise.

In the case of silver and mother-of-pearl, although there is a unity in the reflective awareness of "silver" regarding the property of silverness (*rajatatva*), that cognition is erroneous because it is unstable due to the absence of correspondence regarding the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the connection with the location of the mother-of-pearl, which is subsequently sublated.
Likewise, in the case of the double moon, the cognition is false because it lacks correspondence with the location of the sky.

Through qualities such as sound and the like, there is differentiation among entities; through genus and the like, there is non-differentiation. In this way, both are established within a single cognizer. (IPK 2.3.14)

The experience of the exclusion of difference among entities—based on their verbal forms, shapes, and so forth—and the inclusion of unity by means of universals and the like, is possible only when there is a single cognizer;
moreover, the establishment of mutual difference is dependent upon synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*).

In the Lord who is ultimately real, who is like a perfectly even wall-surface for the painting of the world’s manifold variety, and who is untouched by any contradictory states, [I take refuge]. (IPK 2.3.15)
But when the primordial subject, whose form is eternally manifest, is the locus of all cognition, what new manifestation could serve as a means of knowledge? (IPK 2.3.16)

IPV: Since the manifestation of the unprecedented (*apūrvābhāsa*) establishes an object that was previously unestablished, there is no utility of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), who is eternally manifest.

This is because each respective manifestation constitutes its own respective means of knowledge. Granted, that [means of knowledge] might serve as a means of knowledge for something else, but not for one's own self, which is eternally established.
Rather, the cognizer alone is the [ultimate] authority due to his sovereignty over the act of cognition, being all-pervasive (*vibhu*).
Those various and manifold appearances of the universe arise as diversities within that stable substratum.
By His will, there occurs the emergence and submergence of objects that do not appear as separate from Him, through the power of *māyā-śakti*, which prevents their essential nature from being lost.
In reality, His existence alone is independent and eternal, because of the application of such terms as "contradiction," "prior non-existence," and "subsequent destruction."
As long as he is taught by means of existence and non-existence, he himself assumes the status of a knower; for in the absence of one who desires to teach, instruction is impossible.

"Previously unestablished here, the conventional usage of terms such as 'Īśa' (the Lord) and so forth is now set in motion solely through the manifestation of power, due to the force of delusion. (IPK 2.3.17)

IPV: That conventional usage of terms such as Śiva, Īśvara, and so forth—which has not been applied to this very Self in its nature as the subject (pramātṛ) solely due to the power of delusion caused by *māyā*—is established for the purpose of instruction on contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and the like, by demonstrating causes such as pure sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
Thus ends the third chapter in the section on Action.
And because he possesses infinite power, he manifests these entities in this way by the force of his will; this is his activity, which is his capacity as a creator.
The subject is the Lord, whose nature is consciousness and who possesses infinite power; by the force of his own will, he manifests those various objects in such a manner.
That very power of will is his creative activity, known as the power of the creator.
But for that which is insentient, there is no such power of being whereby the non-existent becomes existent;
therefore, the nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the reality of the agent and the object.
IPV: However, the insentient—such as primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms, or seeds—is not capable of producing what does not exist;
for causality is nothing other than agency, and being an effect is nothing other than being an object of action. Nothing else constitutes these.
That which is non-existent remains non-existent; for that which is non-existent, there can be no nature of existence.
Furthermore, it is said that even for that which exists, there is no further purpose in attaining existence.
In the world, the relationship of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves internally;
its state of being perceivable by both types of sense-faculties arises from the power of some [unmanifest] principle.
IPV: The state of being existent for that which is non-existent is contradictory, whereas it is established for that which is already existent.
The production by the Lord consists precisely in bringing about the state of being perceivable by both the internal and external organs for that which is already established.
Thus, this single action, which exists both internally and externally in succession,
has been established as belonging to one and the same [agent] who is capable of assuming both forms.

This very action, although possessing succession due to its nature as existing both internally and externally, is established as one because it belongs to a single agent—whose existence is proven by self-awareness—and to a single object—which, despite the diversity of the shadows of its manifestations, is to be recollected as a unity; for it has a single substratum non-different from them, and is thus proven to be one.
That which is external is the effect of that very [consciousness], in relation to which there is that which is internal;
and the twofold state of being external and internal is said to exist in relation to the subject.
IPV: The externalization of the object is its state of being an effect (*kāryatva*);

therefore, both externality and the state of being an effect are relative to a single [principle]. With respect to the subject (*pramātṛ*), there is the conventional usage of "internal" and "external. Consequently, it is that very [subject] for whom [the object] is an effect.
Therefore, the Mother alone is the cause; and while abiding as a dual manifestation, she remains as the one [cause] of the effect. Thus, the activity of the One is proclaimed.

IPV: Thus, the cognizer alone is the cause, and he remains one and the same even in the sequence of the manifestation of external and internal effects; in this way as well, the activity of a single agent is established.
For this very reason, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the efficient cause even in the case of a sprout;
otherwise, the causality of other factors such as the seed would not be logically tenable.

IPV: "Production" means the bringing about of external manifestation; thus, the nature of consciousness alone is the cause. Therefore, some maintain that God is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) in the case of sprouts and so forth, nor is it logical for an insentient thing such as a seed to be a cause, as it lacks synthetic awareness (*anusaṃdhāna*).
For instance, a potter produces a jar through his own sovereign power and by means of a specific arrangement, following the sequence of processing various clays and other materials. (IPK 2.4.9)

Even though the potter, as the cognizing subject and the instrumental cause, is present, the jar’s dependence on the preparation of clay and other materials occurs through the boundary known as *niyati* (destiny) created by Īśvara, and not by its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Even for yogins, by the power of their will, that [effect], such as a jar, arises even without clay or seed, performing its respective stable purposeful action. (IPK 2.4.10)
IPV: For yogins, there is the production of stable objects such as jars, which perform purposeful functions, by mere will alone, without depending on clay or other materials.
When the existence of a yogic creation has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition,
the effect or the essential nature [of that object] is a logical reason (hetu) arising from that very source of origination.

Therefore, an effect or an essential nature that contains the implication of its arising from [that cause] is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) when there is no certainty regarding the absence of being produced by a yogi. However, if such certainty exists, then causality would depend upon the necessity of God (*īśvara*).

Furthermore, from the manifestation of fire and so forth belonging solely to that respective subject, there may arise a new manifestation of smoke and so forth, even though it is remote from the sovereign Lord. (IPK 2.4.12)
The effect is the non-deviating mark (*liṅga*) for [the cognition] belonging to another cognizer;
however, the appearance of that [effect] arises from the appearance of that very [cause], while the supreme [cognition] belongs to the sovereign [Lord]. (IPK 2.4.13)
