Even when an appearance of smoke arises preceded by the flashing of an appearance of fire, at a distance and so forth, it is— by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) which has established its capacity from that very appearance of fire common to other various perceivers in that same location— the unerring indicator of that [fire] alone; whereas an appearance of smoke whose conventional status has been established [as such] proceeds, as before, solely from an appearance of smoke belonging to other perceivers— even if that [fire] is imperceptible— due to the absolute disappearance of that appearance of fire and because [the appearance of smoke] exercises sovereignty through its prior [causal] efficacy.
Even that relationship of cause and effect expressed as "this being present,
that exists" is not tenable for the dull-witted who lack [the understanding of] dependence.

IPV: [The opponent argues: "The fixed sequence of 'this being, that comes to be' exists even between the rising of the Kṛttikās and Rohiṇī, though they are not cause and effect; thus, the existence of the latter would follow from the capacity of the former.
And this would not be tenable for dull-witted people who lack mutual dependence.

All that could be said is that the capacity of the former is the existence of the latter, but nothing of the sort has been stated here; nor is the nature of the former, characterized by capacity, identical with the form of the latter's existence."
For this meaning of the locative case is not conceived even in the context of existence or non-existence for those who are restricted solely to their own self and devoid of synthetic reflection.

Whether the effect be existent or non-existent, the cause is likewise limited to itself, insentient, devoid of self-reflection, and by nature independent of anything else; therefore, in this case, the meaning of the case-ending expressing the distinction of qualities (*guṇavibhakti*) based on dependence upon a *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is not tenable.

Therefore, the meaning of the case-ending, which consists of the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva) and rests solely upon the subject (pramātṛ), is logically consistent with the integration of existence (bhāvasamanvaya).

IPV: However, the meaning of the case-endings known as the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva), which is connected to a single cognizer, is logically appropriate as the coordination of earth, seed, water, and so forth; but no other, dry causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is so.
If cause and effect were mutually identical in nature, they would indeed be one; for if there were difference, there could never be the nature of one in the other. (IPK 2.4.17)
If cause and effect were of one another's nature, there would be only oneness, and not their distinct existence as such.
The division of the single self and action following the sequence of time would likewise exist;
thus, agency itself would be such as it transforms through that [action].
IPV: The persistence of that which has a single nature through differentiation is transformation (*pariṇāma*), which is measured by time and is indeed action itself;
therefore, in transformation, the agency of the independent possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is the very cause.
And such [a nature] is not possible for that which is insentient, because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference;
however, it is logical in the case of the single conscious self, due to the diversity of its manifestations.
[Objection: It is improper because it is contradictory for that which is insentient and of undivided nature to exist in a state of differentiation;
[Response: But it is appropriate, because there is no contradiction in a single, transparent conscious self (cidātman) bearing many reflections in this manner.

Even though consciousness is in reality one, there can be no action between two things differentiated by their appearances without the reflective awareness of oneness characterized by the desire to act. (IPK 2.4.20)
IPV: Even though the reality of consciousness is one, a differentiation of appearances cannot occur spontaneously, nor does the state of being an action apply therein.
However, when that conscious Self, desiring to act in such a way, reflects upon itself and manifests [objects] externally, then that [differentiation] becomes possible.
Even for an insentient object, although it possesses this act of existence expressed as "it is," it lacks agency because it lacks autonomy through the application of the desire-to-be (*bubhūṣā*);

therefore, it is the subject alone who brings that object into being, or rather, it is the subject who causes it to exist in such and such a form, such as the Himalayas—this is the ultimate truth here.
In this way, for Him who desires to abide as the world consisting of the appearances of jars, cloths, and so forth, His very will is the cause, the agency, and the action. (IPK 2.4.21)

IPV: For the independent one whose essence is consciousness, the very desire to abide as the Self of the universe is the causality toward the world in the form of agency; that itself is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

Thus, for the single agent whose nature is consciousness, the primary action is that which is called the "will to act" (*cikīrṣā*); there is no object (*karman*) without an agent, since objects and so forth are only metaphorically designated by way of the agent.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the section on Action.

3.1 The First Daily Lesson (Āhnika)
Thus, activity, which functions internally and externally and follows the sequence of time, belongs to the Mother alone; likewise, knowledge and action are inseparable from her.
IPV: Action, which follows a temporal sequence, is precisely the externalization of the Self that resides within the knower; thus, his knowledge and action are mutually inseparable.
However, due to the predominance of the internal state, the reality known as Sādākhya arises first;
but when there is a predominance of external existence, the state of Parameśvara follows after.

Regarding the Lord (īśituḥ) who exists both internally and externally: when internal existence is predominant, it is the principle called Sādākhya; when there is an overflow of external existence, it is the Aiśvara [principle].

Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa), and the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the cognitions of "I" and "this" is Sadvidyā. (IPK 3.1.3)
In the *Iṣṭopadeśa*: "The opening and closing [of the eyes], as well as the states of being external and internal, are indeed Īśvara and Sadāśiva;

because there is no distinction between the external and internal—the object of knowledge and the knower—due to their resting in the single pure consciousness, the cognition of this universe as 'I' through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is Śuddhavidyā."

For those things that have attained the state of "this-ness" and have entered the realm of the knowable, because their essence is consciousness and they are perceived according to their actual state, [they are as they appear]. (IPK 3.1.4)

IPV: Even for those entities that have been brought to the state of being perceived as "this" on the ground of the knowable, there arises the realization of their true nature as "I am this," because their essence is pure consciousness alone; this is the attainment of purity.

In this context, the "inferiority" of entities arises from their appearing as non-self; the "superiority" arises from being veiled by the I-consciousness (ahaṃtā). Indeed, that is the state of the "both superior and inferior" (parāpara).

In this regard, the state of being both transcendent and immanent is as follows: it is "immanent" because the non-I-consciousness (*amatī*) is subordinate, and it is "transcendent" because the entire object of knowledge is veiled by the I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*). Thus, this is a state that is both transcendent and immanent.

Others maintain that even the cognition of difference regarding entities— which arises despite the fact that the agent is of the nature of consciousness— is "vidyā" (knowledge) through the power of māyā alone, just as it is in the case of the Vidyādharas and Īśvaras.
Some say that even though it consists of the agency of awakening, the perception of all things through differentiation is *vidyā*.
This power of *māyā* is indeed *vidyā* itself;
because they have transcended transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the Mantreśvaras and Vidyēśvaras reside therein.
The power of knowledge (*vidyāśakti*) manifests that nature of sovereignty within the state of bondage (*paśubhāva*), while the power called *māyā* again effects concealment.
IPV: For transmigrating beings, the recognition of one's own self as sovereign occurs through *vidyā*, while the state of being a bound animal (*paśu*) occurs through *māyā*.

But when difference appears as of a single flavor, when the non-self is perceived through the sense of "I," and when either the void or the intellect or the body is observed, the power of illusion unfolds. (IPK 3.1.8)

IPV: When entities appear as distinct "this-ness" and the body and so forth appear as the subject "I," then the deluding power of Māyā, the cause of the two-fold error, unfolds from the All-pervasive Lord.
And that cognizer who is empty and so forth, when there is an object of cognition distinct from him,
being himself an object of cognition, is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time.

Furthermore, that cognizer who is distinct from the class of objects of cognition—such as the Void (śūnya) and so forth—is in reality nothing but an object of knowledge (*vedya*), being rendered dependent by the five factors beginning with Time (*kāla*).
Among these, from Time comes the possibility of his past and future states through the manifestation of the present;
from Necessity (*niyati*) comes the determination of the fruits of actions performed.
From passion (*rāga*) arises attachment to enjoyments; from knowledge (*vidyā*) and art (*kalā*), there arise,
even for the insentient and dependent self, limited knowledge and action which are essentially forms of the freedom of consciousness.
That which is to be measured consists of twenty-three principles, comprising both the effects and the instruments;
their undivided form is the one Pradhāna, the root cause. (IPK 3.1.10)
In this context, there is a series of thirteen external and internal instruments, and a group of ten effects, distinguished by their gross and subtle natures. (IPK 3.1.11)
The objects of action (kārya) are twofold:

the five—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which, by virtue of their subtlety, are designated as *tanmātras*; and those which, through mutual aggregation, become gross, such as earth and so forth, as well as the sense organs.
The five organs of action known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals;

and the threefold internal organ consisting of mind, intellect, and ego—this state of fundamental unity of the twenty-three-fold object of knowledge, which comprises both cause and effect, is called *pradhāna*.
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on scripture.
The second daily lesson.
In that regard, Rudra is the presiding deity when one abides in the state of mere subjectivity (mātṛtāmātra);
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established when there is the expansion of differentiated objects of cognition.

In the void, which consists of the *puryaṣṭaka* or even the extremely subtle body, when one remains as pure subjectivity (*pramātṛmātra*) with all other objects of knowledge withdrawn, Rudra is the presiding deity;
whereas when there is the manifestation of distinct objects of knowledge, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are the causes of creation and maintenance.
This cognizer, blinded by māyā, is a transmigrating being bound by karma; when his sovereignty is made manifest by vidyā, he is called liberated, a mass of consciousness. (IPK 3.2.2)
The subject who is bound by illusion is a transmigrating being, dependent on necessity and karma;
through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), by means of the realization of the true nature of the Self, he is liberated.
The subject is called the Lord (pati) when [the objects] exist as his own limbs;
through Māyā, he is the bound soul (paśu), defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth, when [the objects] are differentiated. (IPK 3.2.3)

In the state of sovereignty (*aiśvaryadaśā*), the subject perceives the universe as his own body and is thus the Lord (*pati*); however, in the state of being a bound individual (*puṃstva-avasthā*), he is surrounded by afflictions such as attachment, as well as karma and its latent impressions (*vipākāśaya*), and is thus a bound soul (*paśu*).

The loss of sovereignty of consciousness, and likewise the lack of awareness within sovereignty—this is the twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala), arising from the forfeiture of one's own true nature. (IPK 3.2.4)
The ultimate reality is independent consciousness;
it is full precisely because it possesses such a nature.
By virtue of that very independence, through its own will—and without that independence, without mere consciousness, and without the state of being conscious—it manifests itself as such.

In the case of creation through mere autonomy, because there is a lack of fullness and thus limitation, there is a twofold atomicity; and due to the inversion of the true nature [of the self], this constitutes impurity (*mala*).

Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is that which is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; while the *kārma* [bond] resides in the ignorant agent. All three of these arise solely through the power of *māyā*. (IPK 3.2.5)
IPV: In this very context, when that which is non-different from the two-fold *aṇava* appears as if differentiated, then, due to that very misconception (*viparyāsa*), it is called the *māyīya-mala*.

Because of the misconception regarding the object—the state of being the cause of birth and so forth for even those actions (*karman*) that are themselves causeless—it is the *kārmika-mala*, residing in the agent whose nature is non-awakening (*abodha*).
The will of the Lord in the production of these three impurities is called the power of *māyā*.
Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been emanated by the Lord as distinct from Himself, due to the absence of that agency.
Even for those whose cognition is colored by the object of knowledge (*vedya*), because they are devoid of full agency, their creation by the Lord occurs through a transformation of their own nature.
Even though they are identical in having consciousness alone as their defining characteristic, they are mutually distinct;
likewise, through the differentiation of the Lord’s will, they are known as the Vijñānakevalas.

IPV: Because pure cognitions possess both the nature of consciousness and eternity, they are mutually distinct despite their identity; this is likewise because they are fashioned by the Lord and not otherwise.
And these are called *vijñānakevalas*, being similar to the *puruṣas* of the Sāṃkhya.
But the Pralayākalas, whose nature is the non-cognition of emptiness and so forth, are agents; they possess both the karma-mala and the māyīya-mala, which is conceptualized. (IPK 3.2.8)
In the IPV: "The Pralayakevalins abide as 'I' by transcending the nature of consciousness within the void of the vital breath (śūnyaprāṇa) and so forth.

These individual souls (aṇu) possess the latent impressions of karma (karmasaṃskāra), while the impurity of Māyā (māyāmala) is differentiated according to whether there is a connection with objects of knowledge or not."

Even for those who possess the agency of [limited] cognitions, when the impurity of karma has been destroyed but they still experience diverse objects of knowledge, they are the Vidyeśvaras; these are characterized by the impurity of māyā. (IPK 3.2.9)

Even though they possess agency and have transcended the status of objects for their cognitions, and even though they hold the rank of Vidyeśvaras, because they are still joined with distinct objects of knowledge, the impurity of Māyā certainly remains.
Due to the absence of full agency, they are distinct from Īśvara and from one another as before; for this very reason, they also possess the state of being limited souls (aṇutva).
All living beings, including the gods and others, possess a threefold impurity; even among these, the karmic impurity alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra. (IPK 3.2.10)
For transmigrating beings, from the gods down to the stationary entities, all three impurities exist;
however, it is karma alone that is the actual cause of saṃsāra.

And this very principle of consciousness (cittattva), which consists of agency and is impelled by *kalā*, exists as a limited attribute of the insentient [principles] such as the void (*śūnya*). (IPK 3.2.11)

IPV: Furthermore, this very consciousness-principle (cittattva) of transmigrating beings, which consists of agency, is limited within the insentient [elements] such as the void and vital breath because it is augmented by the power of the Lord’s *kalā* and exists in a subordinate state.
Consequently, it is precisely here that primary atomicity (*aṇutva*) resides.

The primacy of agency and of consciousness belonging to the conscious self (cidātman) is present even in the void and other such qualities; knowledge of that [primacy] is characterized by absorption into it. (IPK 3.2.12)

IPV: Furthermore, when these very [states] such as emptiness (śūnya) exist as subordinate to the consciousness that is the self as agent, then for this cognizer—who has attained the nature of being composed of that consciousness—this is called "knowledge," characterized by the immersion into its power.

In that which is empty—whose nature is the absence of cognition and so forth, which is the locus of "I-ness" and agency, and which contains only the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of indistinct forms—there is the emptiness of the knowable. (IPK 3.2.13)

IPV: When subjectivity arises through the conceit of "I-ness" (ahaṃtābhimāna) based merely on the negation of intellect, vital breath, and so forth, then, even though that much remains in deep sleep, there is an absence of objects of knowledge; for although a latent impression (saṃskāra) may exist, it is not perceived due to its formless nature.
By this alone, [the state] is distinguished from the Puruṣa of the Sāṃkhya.
The internal function of the senses is considered to be that which impels the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth;
it is called "life" (jīvana), or else it is the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) within the vital breath, consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka). (IPK 3.2.14)

IPV: This very subject of emptiness (*śūnyapramātā*), whose internal activity consists in the impelling of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—which are termed "life" and are common to the powers of all the senses—is called the "living being" (*jīva*).

The state of being the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭakatva*) belongs either to those powers of the senses together with the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*), or else to the state of being the eightfold city by virtue of the subjecthood of the vital breath and the sense of "I."
When one remains in that state alone, it is called the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta), which is comparable to cosmic dissolution (pralaya);
it may be with objective experience (savedya) or without objective experience (apavedya), and may be joined with or free from the impurity of māyā.
In the state of abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because there is no object of cognition (*vedya*), there is an absence of the impurity of *māyā*;

however, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, due to the connection with objects of cognition such as the touch of pleasure, there is a state like deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), similar to dissolution (*pralaya*), just like the impurity of *māyā*.
Even though it lies within the path of the mind alone, because of the delusion that it is an object of the senses, the vivid manifestation of entities is considered the state of dream. (IPK 3.2.16)

Even when the capacities of the sense organs, such as the eye, are not functioning, the manifestation of forms and so forth created by the Lord through the power of the mind alone constitutes the state of dreaming for the individual soul (*aṇu*).
This is an illusion because it persists only for a short duration, lacking continuity over time, unlike the manifestations of forms and so forth that are common to other subjects.
That common creation which, existing externally as the object of all the senses, is stable for all subjects—that is waking. (IPK 3.2.17)
IPV: Creation is the waking state, produced by the power of all internal and external faculties;
therein, as before, there is the delusion of two moons and so forth.

This triad [of body, speech, and mind] is to be abandoned because the agency [of the Self] resides primarily in the vital breath and the rest; for [the Self] is joined with pleasure, pain, and so forth, which consist chiefly in the loss or increase of those [functions]. (IPK 3.2.18)

IPV: These states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—believed by one who identifies with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth as being the Self—are to be abandoned due to the excess [of identification] and the consequent loss of autonomy.
The increase of autonomy, even in its slightest degree, consists of pleasure, joy, and the like; likewise, its deficiency consists of pain, aversion, and the like.
The entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), whose essence is the enjoyment of objects, is bondage.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and in-breath (*apāna*), each of which functions during both sleep and waking;
that which consists of their cessation is called the equalizing breath (*samāna*), as it does during deep sleep and at the equinoxes.

And that self of breath (prāṇātman), which in the waking state consists of prāṇa and apāna in the form of inhalation and exhalation, is called "samāna" in deep sleep— at this stage, because of the obstruction of their deficiency or excess, like the equinox (viṣuvat) when night and day are equal.
The one moving through the middle and upwards, called udāna, resides in the fourth state and consists of fire;
it is Vijñānākala, the Lord of Mantras. Vyāna, which is the supreme, is the soul of the universe. (IPK 3.2.20)

The *udāna* is so called because it rises upward through the flow of the central path (*madhyamārga*), having attained unity by cutting off the lateral flows of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* in both flanks.
Because it occupies the upper portion like the central channel, it possesses the nature of fire in the fourth state (*turyadaśā*).

In the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), which is full and unconditioned by space and time, it abandons its state of flowing and exists in a state of absolute intensity; this is designated as *vyāna*.
And this pair of ten states is to be accepted, because the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) exists as being virtually identical to the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the second chapter in the section on scripture.
Thus ends the section on scripture.
4. The Section on the Compendium of Reality.
One's own self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings; it is I, whose form is the universe, strengthened by the undivided awareness that "this is I. (IPK 4.1)

In the first stage of the process of reception, the one Self—which is common to all living beings and whose nature is the universe—is nourished by the wonder of the fusion between the undivided subject and the undivided object.

Within that state, in the portion consisting of this "this-world" (idaṃbhāga) created by itself, it is brought to the state of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃkāra-parāmarśa) by means of the subject-aspect of the intellect and so forth. (IPK 4.2)

IPV: When that reflective awareness of "this-ness" (idaṃtā) has emerged from this yawning state of Maheśvara, that which is manifested as the object of perception—namely, the intellect (buddhi), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the void (śūnya)—takes on the form of a specific portion of the knowable; by being brought under the purview of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), it is rendered a limited subject.
The individual soul is considered to be manifold, consisting of the non-recognition of its own true nature.
In that state of emanation, there are activity and bliss, and experience consists of suffering and pleasure. (IPK 4.3)
IPV: This very act of making the Universal Self appear limited is called non-recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*).

Thus, the reflective awareness of the subordinate ego-sense (*aparāhaṃkāra*) residing within the various fragments of intellect, vital breath, and so forth, is designated as "non-cognition of the Supreme" (*parāparijñāna*).
There are many individual selves (*pratyakātman*), [but they are not the one].
Within those forms of subjects, Maheśvara has created his own bliss (*svānanda*) in accordance with his own action and sole agency.

That very thing is experience (*bhoga*), known as a fragment of bliss (*ānandaleśa*) and designated as pleasure; yet it consists of a trace of action and is of the nature of suffering, for action and suffering will be explained [later].

In the case of the Lord, that which constitutes knowledge and action regarding entities that are the forms of his own body, together with Māyā as the third, are precisely what constitute *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* in the bound soul (*paśu*). (IPK 4.4)
In the individual soul (paśu), the powers of knowledge and action belonging to God are, through Māyā, [transformed into] the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Established in differentiation, the state of being power (*śaktitva*) is not predicated of these qualities (*guṇas*), which are subject to transformation as instruments and effects, for one who possesses power (*śāktimataḥ*). (IPK 4.5)

IPV: Furthermore, because the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* appear as distinct, they are not designated as "powers" (*śakti*), since there is no difference between power and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).
In reality, the universe is the expansion of power.
Existence is bliss; activity belongs to the Lord, while its absence belongs to the bound soul (paśu).
That which consists of both is passion (rajas), which is suffering, being a confluence of purity (sattva) and darkness (tamas). (IPK 4.6)

In the Ipv, the infinite agency of Īśvara is described as a wondrous activity consisting of supreme light and bliss (*prakāśānandamayi*); however, in the case of the *pratyagātman*, that very light and bliss, when they have become objects of perception, are called *sattva*. And the absence thereof is *tamas*.
Both *sattva* and *tamas*, whose natures are respectively illumination and bliss and their respective absences, are of the nature of union;
for the bound soul (*paśu*), this is designated as *rajas*, and is called both activity and suffering.
Even those [cognitions] of the Lord which arise from non-temporal reflective awareness of "this-ness" appear variegated in that manner, both mixed and distinct. (IPK 4.7)

Moreover, those entities which, even without the application of the conventional designation "this" (idaṃśabda-saṃketa) by Maheśvara, are indicated as "this" in the state of childhood because manifestation has the essence of reflective awareness (parāmarśa)—

they manifest as having various forms, being distinct from their own particular nature (svalakṣaṇa) in the form of universals through their co-referentiality with multiple appearances, because they are thus created by Him.

But those objects which appear as distinct must be imagined as belonging to the inner self (pratyagātman) within the sphere of memory, imagination, and so forth, under their respective diverse designations.

IPV: Those objects, which consist of a universal nature yet appear as distinct manifestations, are presented in memory by the *kṣetrajñas*— who possess selves made manifest through various designations such as "I am thin," "I am suffering," or "I am happy," due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) left by the experience of those objects— as being capable of internal reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*) under their respective names, such as "jar," "silver," "white cloth," or "cart," by means of the power of conceptualization (*vikalpana*).
When there is no loss of prior experience,
[the manifestation occurs] through independence in various forms of imaginative construction and the like.
This very appearance of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, consisting of words, constitutes the bondage of saṃsāra in the state of a bound soul (paśu).
His unique creation, which subsists upon the creation of the Lord, is indeed real due to his ignorance, by virtue of the power of the Lord who is identical with that [creation]. (IPK 4.9)

By means of the activity of conceptualization—which is of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is immovable in order to obstruct its own repose, and which takes the form of the variety of various phonemes— [the state of the Self is obscured]. (IPK 4.10)

The *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), being indeed of the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*), creates through the very power of the Lord—which remains unrecognized—objects that take on various universal forms; these are objects common to all yet perceivable only by him.

And that power of the Lord, which is designated as *māyā* because it obstructs [the soul's] resting solely within its own self, undergoes a state of flux in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through hundreds of infinite enumerations of the distinctions among phonemes such as 'ka' and so forth; thus, through its operation known as *vikalpa* (conceptualization), it projects objects internally.
This creation of Īśvara is both common and otherwise, due to its clear manifestation;
through the one-pointedness that abandons conceptual construction, one gradually attains the state of lordship. (IPK 4.11)

However, the creation of the Lord (Īśvara) is common to all subjects (*pramātṛ*), because they arise right within that [creation]; whereas the creation restricted to a single subject—such as in dreams or delusions—is due to the immersion (*āveśa*) of that single subject.

And that [creation] consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I am this," which, because no differentiation has arisen, is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and possesses a clear manifestation.

In that regard, through the repeated practice of diminishing the conceptualization of the activities of the *kṣetrajña* as they arise from time to time, there occurs for transmigrating beings the liberation of the state of being a *kṣetrajña* due to the gradual emergence of sovereign power of a single flavor.

For one who fully understands, "All this manifestation is mine," there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of conceptual constructions regarding the universal self. (IPK 4.12)

Even for the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), the initiation of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) occurs solely through the power of the Lord; therefore, even in that state, for one who has fully realized their nature as the Lord and who enters the universe non-dually with the thought, "This manifestation consisting of transmigratory existence is mine," there is nothing other than the state of the Great Lord (*maheśvaratā*), because they produce all conceptual constructions merely through reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
The liberated one perceives this common object as non-different from his own self, just like Maheśvara; whereas the bound one perceives it again as being absolutely different. (Ipk 4.13)
The object of knowledge is one for both the bound and the liberated;
however, the bound knows it as something of absolute distinction, whereas the liberated knows it as his own self-body.
In every respect, however, Śiva is filled with the flood of infinite principles merged within him; he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme syllable.
IPV: But when the object of knowledge has completely dissolved within and the "I-consciousness" is full, there is nothing but Śiva-hood.
Thus, knowing his own self as well as its right knowledge and action, and perceiving them according to his desire, he both knows and acts. (IPK 4.15)

Thus, having recognized the Self as the Lord—who has manifested the knowledge of His powers and who is replete with infinite powers of knowledge and action—one sees and creates everything according to one's will.
Thus has this easily accessible new path been revealed by me, just as it was taught by the Great Teachers in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise.
Therefore, one who places his feet upon this [path], realizing his own agency over the universe and constantly entering into that which consists of the nature of Śiva, attains perfection.

IPV: Wherein, within ordinary worldly discourse exactly as it stands, the attainment of the state of Śiva occurs through mere recognition— this very straight and novel path has been pointed out by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrī Somānanda, who had directly realized the form of the Supreme Lord Bhaṭṭāraka, in his treatise named *Śivadṛṣṭi*, and has been made to reach the heart by me through the application of reasoning.
By the thorough cultivation of this, through the immersion into the state of Śiva, one becomes liberated even while living.

Just as the beloved of a slender woman, though standing near her, was not able to give her pleasure because he was perceived by her as being no different from any other man despite her various entreaties;

so too, the Lord of the Universe, though his own self, is not sufficient for his own manifestation of glory because his qualities are not recognized by the world. Therefore, this [treatise] called *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) has been composed.
Moreover, by means of the analogy of the beloved woman, the recognition of the Lord (īśvarapratyabhijñā) is to be established, which yields a result never before attained.
For the sake of the effortless accomplishment [of the goal] for people, this Recognition of the Lord (Īśvarapratyabhijñā) has been established by Utpaladeva, the son of Udayākara. (IPK 4.18)
IVp: This path to accomplishment, which is easy to attain, has been revealed.
Thus ends the chapter on the Compendium of Reality.
This Commentary on the Recognition of the Lord is completed.
